specPoints.text: describe the combustion of elements in oxygen, including magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur

primer.text: From Composition of Air you already know that oxygen makes up about one-fifth of the air and supports burning. This note names the process properly, shows why every such reaction releases heat, and works through the three combustions you must be able to describe, for magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur, with their observations and symbol equations.

lessons.title: What is combustion?
lessons.opening: Combustion is the scientific word for burning, and every combustion reaction involves oxygen reacting with an element or a compound to produce oxides. These reactions always give out heat, which makes them exothermic. They can equally be described as oxidation reactions, since the burning substance gains oxygen.
keyPoints: Combustion is the scientific word for burning.
Every combustion reaction involves oxygen reacting with an element or compound to produce oxides.
Combustion reactions give out heat, so they are always exothermic.
The same reactions also count as oxidation reactions, since oxygen is gained.
The three combustions of record for this course are magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur in oxygen.

low.restatement: Burning means joining something to oxygen, and the products are always oxides. The reaction warms its surroundings, which is why a flame is hot and why combustion is called exothermic.
low.analogy: Think of oxygen as the one guest every fire invites; whether the fuel is metal, gas or powder, the product party is always oxides.
low.examPointer: Use the proper terms in answers: combustion, oxides, exothermic, and the classification as oxidation reactions.

medium.restatement: Combustion is the reaction of an element or compound with oxygen forming oxides, and it is exothermic because energy is released to the surroundings as heat. The same reactions double as oxidation reactions, since the burning species gains oxygen in the process.
medium.analogy: Picture oxygen as a strict landlord who only accepts full payment in the currency of oxides, and pays back the rent as heat every single time.
medium.examPointer: Questions often ask why combustion warms the surroundings; answer that energy is released by the reaction, which is the meaning of exothermic.

check.stem: What is always produced when an element burns in oxygen?

options.text: An oxide of the element
options.explanation: Combustion joins the element to oxygen, and the compound formed is by definition that element's oxide.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, whatever the element
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide only forms when the burning element is carbon; other elements give their own oxides.
options.misconception: one product assumed for all fuels

options.text: Water, whatever the element
options.explanation: Water is the product only for hydrogen; magnesium gives magnesium oxide and sulfur gives sulfur dioxide.

options.text: Nothing new forms, the element simply gets hot
options.explanation: Combustion is a chemical change with a new substance made; heat alone would be physical, not combustion.

check.stem: Why are all combustion reactions classed as exothermic?

options.text: Because they give out heat to the surroundings
options.explanation: Exothermic means energy leaves the reaction for the surroundings, and every combustion warms what is around it.

options.text: Because they need a flame to start them
options.explanation: A flame may be needed for ignition, but the classification describes the energy given out during the reaction itself.

options.text: Because oxygen is a cold gas that must be heated
options.explanation: The temperature of a reactant does not define the energy change; the heat given out does.
options.misconception: reactant temperature mistaken for the classification

options.text: Because the oxides formed are always hot solids
options.explanation: Oxides can be solids, liquids or gases; the exothermic label refers to heat released, not to the product's state.
options.misconception: product state confused with energy change

check.stem: In what other way can combustion reactions be classified?

options.text: As oxidation reactions
options.explanation: The burning substance gains oxygen, which is exactly the definition of oxidation.

options.text: As neutralisation reactions
options.explanation: Neutralisation pairs an acid with a base; no acid or base is required for combustion.

options.text: As displacement reactions
options.explanation: Displacement swaps one element for another in a compound; combustion simply adds oxygen.

options.text: As thermal decomposition reactions
options.explanation: Decomposition breaks one substance into others using heat; combustion builds oxides and releases heat.

check.stem: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to give water. Which classification set fits this reaction completely?

options.text: Combustion, oxidation and exothermic
options.explanation: Hydrogen burns in oxygen (combustion), gains oxygen (oxidation), and releases heat (exothermic), so all three labels fit.

options.text: Combustion only, because water is the product
options.explanation: The product does not limit the classification; the gain of oxygen and the heat release both still apply.

options.text: Endothermic and oxidation
options.explanation: Hydrogen combustion is famously exothermic; endothermic would mean it absorbed heat instead.

options.text: Displacement and neutralisation
options.explanation: Neither family describes adding oxygen to an element; both labels are wrong here.

check.stem: A candle burns in a closed jar and the flame goes out. What has happened to the oxygen?

options.text: It has been used up by the combustion, forming oxides, so burning can no longer continue
options.explanation: Combustion consumes oxygen; once the share inside the jar is gone, the reaction has nothing left to react with.

options.text: The oxygen has turned into nitrogen
options.explanation: Elements do not transmute in a flame; the oxygen ends up locked inside oxide products.

options.text: The oxygen has escaped through the glass
options.explanation: A closed jar holds its gases; the disappearance is consumption by the reaction, not leakage.

options.text: The oxygen has melted into the wax
options.explanation: Oxygen reacts with the burning material to form oxides; it does not simply dissolve away into the fuel.

lessons.title: The combustion reactions of Mg, H2 & S
sourceHeadings: The combustion reactions of Mg, H2 & S
lessons.opening: Three element combustions are required knowledge: magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur, each burning in oxygen gas. Magnesium burns with an intense white flame leaving white magnesium oxide powder, hydrogen burns exothermically to give water, and sulfur burns with a blue flame to a colourless, poisonous gas. Each reaction has its own visible signs, paired with a symbol equation you should be able to write.
keyPoints: Magnesium burns with an intense white flame and white magnesium oxide powder is produced.
Hydrogen burns exothermically in oxygen and water is produced.
Sulfur burns with a blue flame and a colourless, poisonous gas is produced, by S (s) + O2 (g) → SO2 (g).

low.restatement: Magnesium gives a blinding white flame and a white powder; hydrogen burns to water; sulfur gives a blue flame and a choking colourless gas. Learn the visible signs and the equation together for each element.
low.analogy: Three different fireworks from one same oxygen supply: the fuel decides the colour, the product and the equation.
low.examPointer: Match observations to equations in both directions; questions may give the flame colour and ask for the product, or the reverse.

medium.restatement: Each combustion follows the same pattern of element plus oxygen forming an oxide, balanced as 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O and S + O2 → SO2. The visible signs distinguish them: the intense white flame of magnesium, the exothermic burn of hydrogen to water, and sulfur's blue flame with its colourless poisonous dioxide.
medium.analogy: Think of one recipe, element plus oxygen, cooked three ways: the same oven (oxygen), three dishes (oxide products), three signature looks (observations).
medium.examPointer: Balancing is examinable: check atom counts on both sides of each equation, and include state symbols where the question asks.

check.stem: Which observation identifies the combustion of magnesium in oxygen?

options.text: An intense white flame with white powder produced
options.explanation: Magnesium burns with a fierce white flame and leaves the white powder magnesium oxide.

options.text: A blue flame with a colourless gas produced
options.explanation: That pair describes sulfur; magnesium's signature is the white flame and white solid.

options.text: A pale green flame with a dense gas produced
options.explanation: No such combustion is on the list; pale green in solution belongs to chlorine chemistry, not burning magnesium.

options.text: No flame, but the metal slowly tarnishes
options.explanation: Slow tarnish is ordinary oxidation in air; combustion of magnesium is fast, bright and fierce.

check.stem: What is the product of burning hydrogen in oxygen?

options.text: Water
options.explanation: Hydrogen plus oxygen forms H2O, and the balanced equation is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

options.text: Hydrogen oxide powder
options.explanation: Hydrogen's oxide is water itself, a liquid turned to vapour in the hot flame, not a powder.

options.text: Oxygen gas, because hydrogen acts as a catalyst
options.explanation: Hydrogen is a reactant here, not a catalyst; both elements are consumed making water.

options.text: Hydrogen peroxide
options.explanation: H2O2 is a different compound with an extra oxygen; burning hydrogen gives plain water.

check.stem: Which equation is the correct symbol equation for burning sulfur in oxygen?

options.text: S (s) + O2 (g) → SO2 (g)
options.explanation: One sulfur atom joins one oxygen molecule to give one sulfur dioxide molecule, already balanced as written.

options.text: S (s) + O2 (g) → SO3 (g)
options.explanation: Sulfur trioxide needs an extra step with a catalyst; direct combustion of sulfur gives the dioxide.
options.misconception: oxide chosen one oxygen too rich

options.explanation: This would need two oxygens on the left to balance; as written the atoms do not match.

options.text: S (s) + O (g) → SO (g)
options.explanation: Oxygen exists as diatomic O2 molecules; equations must use the molecular form of the element.

check.stem: Why is the gas from burning sulfur described as dangerous?

options.text: Because the colourless sulfur dioxide produced is poisonous
options.explanation: SO2 is toxic and irritant, and being colourless it gives no visual warning of its presence.

options.text: Because the gas is explosive on contact with air
options.explanation: The gas is not explosive; its hazard is toxicity, which is why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.

options.text: Because it is a heavy liquid that floods the bench
options.explanation: The product is a gas, not a liquid; its danger comes from being breathed in.

options.text: Because it burns a second time with a hotter flame
options.explanation: The dioxide does not reignite; the hazard to describe is its poisonous nature.

check.stem: A student writes the magnesium equation as Mg + O2 → MgO. What correction is needed?

options.text: Balance it as 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO so the oxygen atoms match on both sides
options.explanation: Two oxygen atoms enter from O2, so two MgO units must leave, requiring two magnesium atoms.

options.text: Change O2 to O, because equations use single atoms
options.explanation: Oxygen exists as diatomic molecules; the O2 must stay and the coefficients do the balancing.
options.misconception: diatomic oxygen rewritten as single atoms

options.text: It is already balanced and needs no correction
options.explanation: One O2 supplies two oxygens but only one MgO accepts them, so the equation as written is unbalanced.

options.text: Add heat on the right-hand side to balance the energy
options.explanation: Energy terms are not atoms; balancing counts atoms of each element, not heat.

glossary.definition: The scientific word for burning: a reaction in which oxygen reacts with an element or compound to produce oxides.
The compound formed when an element reacts with oxygen, such as magnesium oxide or sulfur dioxide.
Describes a reaction that gives out heat to the surroundings, as every combustion does.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen; combustion is therefore also an oxidation reaction.
A balanced equation written in chemical formulae and state symbols rather than words.

workedExample.prompt: For each combustion of record, give the observation and the balanced symbol equation: a) magnesium in oxygen; b) hydrogen in oxygen; c) sulfur in oxygen. d) Why can all three reactions also be classified as oxidation reactions?
steps: a) Magnesium burns with an intense white flame leaving white powder: 2Mg (s) + O2 (g) → 2MgO (s).
b) Hydrogen burns exothermically and water is produced: 2H2 (g) + O2 (g) → 2H2O (g).
c) Sulfur burns with a blue flame giving a colourless, poisonous gas: S (s) + O2 (g) → SO2 (g).
d) In each reaction the burning substance gains oxygen, so every combustion is also an oxidation reaction (and all are exothermic).
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) White flame and powder; 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. b) Water forms; 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. c) Blue flame, SO2; S + O2 → SO2. d) Oxygen is gained — combustion is oxidation.
